Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

derivations.claim: Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula.

Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables.

For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent.

Put $\theta=\lambda|A|$. The count mass in step 3.1 gives, by nonnegative partial sums and [F5],
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{an}e^{-\theta}\frac{\theta^n}{n!}=e^{-\theta}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta e^a)^n}{n!}=\exp\!\left(\theta(e^a-1)\right).$$
For $\theta=0$, the count is zero almost surely and both sides are one, so no ambiguous zero power is needed. This establishes the exponential-moment interface before entropy estimates use it.

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves.

For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. Thus the laws agree on every finite count cylinder. These cylinders generate the configuration sigma-algebra by [F4], and pi-lambda uniqueness identifies the laws. The one-set count law gives $E_{Q_\lambda}N_A=\lambda|A|$ for bounded $A$. For arbitrary Borel $A$, increase bounded cubes to all space and apply [F5] to the counting measures and Lebesgue measure to obtain the same extended identity. For disjoint Borel $A_n$, the pointwise counting identity $N_{\cup_n A_n}=\sum_nN_{A_n}$ and [F5] show countable additivity of $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}$, while the empty set has expectation zero. Thus the defined intensity functional is a measure and equals $\lambda$ times Lebesgue measure.

Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

boundaries.evidence: The statement includes one bounded Borel set, giving a Poisson count with mean λ times its volume.
The statement includes empty partition atoms and null Borel sets; their zero counts do not disrupt the product law.

Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$.

In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity.

If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality.

Finiteness of $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)$ gives a joint density and its conditional kernel by [F2]. Pushing forward by $(s,y)\mapsto(r(s),y)$ and using step 4.1 gives finite $D(P_{R,Y}\Vert P_R\otimes Q_Y)$, so [F2] supplies the corresponding conditional kernel for $R$ as well. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for random variables $R,S,Y$ taking values in standard-Borel spaces $\mathcal R,\mathcal S,\mathcal Y$, with $R=r(S)$ for a measurable $r:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$, and a probability reference $Q_Y$ on $\mathcal Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)<\infty$.

derivations.claim: If $b$ solves the system and $\lambda_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jc_j=0$, multiply row $j$ by $\lambda_j$ and add the finitely many inequalities. The left side is $(\sum_j\lambda_jc_j)\cdot b=0$ by [F2]; hence $0\ge\sum_j\lambda_jh_j$. This proves necessity.

For sufficiency, prove by induction on $n$ the alternative: if the finite system has no solution, there is a nonnegative combination of its rows whose coefficient vector is zero and whose right side is positive. If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent.

Let $n>0$ and assume the alternative for $n-1$ variables. Write $c_j=(a_j,\alpha_j)$ with $a_j\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and split the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive.

The reduced system in $u\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ is feasible exactly when the original is. Indeed, a solution $(u,t)$ implies every retained inequality; adding row $p$ multiplied by $-\alpha_q>0$ to row $q$ multiplied by $\alpha_p>0$ cancels $t$ and gives each pair row. Conversely, if $u$ satisfies the reduced system, rows in $P$ impose finitely many lower bounds $t\ge(h_p-a_p\cdot u)/\alpha_p$, and rows in $N$ impose finitely many upper bounds $t\le(h_q-a_q\cdot u)/\alpha_q$. Each pair row is exactly the inequality that its lower bound is no greater than its upper bound. If both sets are nonempty, their finite maximum lower bound is at most their finite minimum upper bound, so choose $t$ between them. If only lower bounds occur choose their maximum; if only upper bounds occur choose their minimum; if neither occurs choose $t=0$. Thus the original system has a solution.

If the original system is infeasible, step 2.1 makes the reduced system infeasible. By induction there are nonnegative multipliers on reduced rows with zero combined first $n-1$ coordinates and positive combined right side. Lift each retained zero-row multiplier to its original row; lift each pair-row multiplier $\mu_{pq}$ to coefficients $-\alpha_q\mu_{pq}$ on row $p$ and $\alpha_p\mu_{pq}$ on row $q$. All lifted coefficients are nonnegative. Every pair lift has last coordinate $(-\alpha_q)\alpha_p+\alpha_p\alpha_q=0$; the total first coordinates vanish by the reduced certificate, and its right side remains positive. This is the required certificate for the original system and completes the induction.

If the stated multiplier condition holds, the certificate from step 3.1 cannot exist, because it would have zero combined left coefficient and positive combined right side. Therefore the system is feasible. Together with step 1.1 this proves both directions, including the empty-variable base case in step 1.2, the zero/positive/negative sign partition and bound reconstruction in steps 1.3–2.1, and the lifted certificate in step 3.1.

For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For $\omega=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)$, write $H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. For $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, let $\zeta_n^{\rm out}=\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n$ and define the finite-volume boundary Hamiltonian
$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Fix a closed system $s$ of constitution $c$, with equilibrium domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], and fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$. Define, for $x\in D_c$,
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U_c(x)+p_0V_c(x)-T_0S_c(x),
$$
where $U_c,V_c$ are the dimensioned energy and volume maps of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and $S_c$ is the adopted entropy of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Thus $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ has units joules.

Let $P_s\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ be an admitted closed system process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with system endpoints $x_{P_s}^-,x_{P_s}^+\in D_c$. Let $R$ be its ideal thermal reservoir and $B$ its ideal pressure store; both lie inside a declared isolated-compound outer boundary. Let $\widehat P$ be an admitted process record for that isolated compound. By an extension, require that $\widehat P$ has the same time interval, system endpoints, system configuration path, and system-side protocol and transfer records as $P_s$, together with the reservoir and store records. Write its compound endpoint association as
$$
\rho_{\widehat P}(\pm)=(x_{P_s}^\pm,y_R^\pm,y_B^\pm)\in\mathcal F\subseteq D_c\times Y_R\times Y_B,
$$
where $Y_R,Y_B$ are the model-declared reservoir and store state sets and $\mathcal F$ is the exact feasible endpoint set from [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The system protocol assigns heat $Q[P_s]$ and work $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ to $P_s$; the auxiliary endpoint changes in $\widehat P$ satisfy the reservoir and store relations in [A1]–[A2] below. No matter crosses the compound boundary, no work channel other than pressure-store work acts on the system, and no other energy-coordinate changes are omitted.

Then the system endpoint difference obeys
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)\le0.
$$
If the final compound endpoint $\rho_{\widehat P}(+)$ is an attained global entropy maximum on $\mathcal F$, then $x_{P_s}^+$ attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the system projection
$$
\Pi_s(\mathcal F):=\{x\in D_c:\exists y_R\in Y_R,\ y_B\in Y_B\text{ with }(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F\}.
$$
This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

Fix a closed system $s$ of constitution $c$, with equilibrium domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], and fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$. Define, for $x\in D_c$,
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U_c(x)+p_0V_c(x)-T_0S_c(x),
$$
where $U_c,V_c$ are the dimensioned energy and volume maps of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and $S_c$ is the adopted entropy of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Thus $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ has units joules.

Let $P_s\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ be an admitted closed system process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with system endpoints $x_{P_s}^-,x_{P_s}^+\in D_c$. Let $R$ be its ideal thermal reservoir and $B$ its ideal pressure store; both lie inside a declared isolated-compound outer boundary. Let $\widehat P$ be an admitted process record for that isolated compound. By an extension, require that $\widehat P$ has the same time interval, system endpoints, system configuration path, and system-side protocol and transfer records as $P_s$, together with the reservoir and store records. Write its compound endpoint association as
$$
\rho_{\widehat P}(\pm)=(x_{P_s}^\pm,y_R^\pm,y_B^\pm)\in\mathcal F\subseteq D_c\times Y_R\times Y_B,
$$
where $Y_R,Y_B$ are the model-declared reservoir and store state sets and $\mathcal F$ is the exact feasible endpoint set from [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The system protocol assigns heat $Q[P_s]$ and work $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ to $P_s$; the auxiliary endpoint changes in $\widehat P$ satisfy the reservoir and store relations in [A1]–[A2] below. No matter crosses the compound boundary, no work channel other than pressure-store work acts on the system, and no other energy-coordinate changes are omitted.

Then the system endpoint difference obeys
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)\le0.
$$
If the final compound endpoint $\rho_{\widehat P}(+)$ is an attained global entropy maximum on $\mathcal F$, then $x_{P_s}^+$ attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the system projection
$$
\Pi_s(\mathcal F):=\{x\in D_c:\exists y_R\in Y_R,\ y_B\in Y_B\text{ with }(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F\}.
$$
This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. The nonnegative integral defined by
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] equals the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral
defined by [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], with the same value in
$[0,+\infty]$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: The map $h$ is continuous, so [L2] makes $H$ compact. For every Borel probability $P$ on $K$, each coordinate of $h$ is bounded and Borel. Compactness and [L1] give boundedness. If $|f|\le M$ for one such coordinate, [F3] gives $\int_K|f|\,dP\le M P(K)=M$, so $f$ is integrable.

Every point of $C$ is a finite convex combination of points $h(x_i)$. If such a representation has $N>d+2$, the linear map $T:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+2}$ defined by $T(c)=(\sum_i c_i h(x_i),\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector $c$ by [L3], because the coordinate bases give domain dimension $N$ and codomain dimension $d+2$. Thus $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i h(x_i)=0$, so $c$ has both positive and negative coordinates. After dropping zero weights from the representation, set $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace each weight $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. The new weights remain nonnegative, still sum to one, represent the same point, and at least one is zero. Repeating reduces every combination to at most $d+2$ terms. Hence $C$ is the image of $K^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$ under $\Theta((x_i),(\theta_i))=\sum_{i=1}^{d+2}\theta_i h(x_i)$, where $\Delta_{d+2}:=\{(\theta_i):\theta_i\ge0,\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; shorter combinations are padded with zero weights and any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Each factor $K$ is closed and bounded by [L2], and $\Delta_{d+2}$ is closed by continuity of the finite coordinate sum and its coordinate inequalities; it is bounded since $0\le\theta_i\le1$. Their product is therefore closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{(d+1)(d+2)}$, so compact by [L2]. To check $\Theta$ is continuous on this compact parameter set, fix a parameter $((x_i),(\theta_i))$. Each coordinate $h_j$ is bounded by some $M$ on $K$ and is continuous at each of the finitely many $x_i$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose neighborhoods of the $x_i$ making $|h_j(x_i')-h_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/(2N)$ for every output coordinate $j$, and require $|\theta_i'-\theta_i|<\epsilon/(2N(M+1))$. Since $0\le\theta_i'\le1$ and $|h_j(x_i)|\le M$, each product difference $|\theta_i'h_j(x_i')-\theta_ih_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/N$; summing over $i$ makes each output-coordinate difference smaller than $\epsilon$. Thus $\Theta$ is continuous. The continuous-image clause of [L2] makes its image $C$ compact, and [L2] also makes $C$ closed.

Fix any Borel probability $P$ on $K$ and let $y(P):=(\int_K x\,dP,\int_Ks\,dP)=\int_Kh\,dP$, with coordinatewise integration. For $\epsilon>0$, compactness of $H$ gives a finite cover of $H$ by open Euclidean balls of radius $\epsilon$. Their preimages under $h$ are Borel; disjointifying them in a fixed finite order gives a finite Borel partition $(A_i)$ of $K$. For every nonempty part choose $z_i\in A_i$ and put $\theta_i=P(A_i)$. Then $y_\epsilon:=\sum_i\theta_i h(z_i)$ belongs to $C$. For $x\in A_i$, both $h(x)$ and $h(z_i)$ lie in the same radius-$\epsilon$ ball, so each coordinate difference is at most $2\epsilon$. The simple map equal to $h(z_i)$ on $A_i$ has integral $y_\epsilon$ by the simple-integral definition. By linearity and the integral triangle inequality in [F3], each coordinate of $y(P)-y_\epsilon$ has absolute value at most $2\epsilon\sum_iP(A_i)=2\epsilon$. Consequently $\|y(P)-y_\epsilon\|_2\le2\epsilon\sqrt{d+1}$, so the sequence obtained with $\epsilon=1/n$ converges to $y(P)$. Since $C$ is closed by step 2.1, $y(P)\in C$.

Because $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, a finite convex combination of generators has barycenter $\bar x$; its corresponding combination of points $h(x)$ shows that $E_{\bar x}:=\{r\in\mathbb R:(\bar x,r)\in C\}$ is nonempty. The set $E_{\bar x}$ is bounded because $C$ is bounded, and it is closed because $C$ is closed and $r\mapsto(\bar x,r)$ is continuous. By [L2] it is compact in $\mathbb R$, so [L1] applied to the identity function yields a maximum $r_*\in E_{\bar x}$.

Represent $(\bar x,r_*)\in C$ by a finite convex combination $\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i(x_i,s(x_i))$, dropping zero weights. If $N>d+1$, the linear map $R:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ given by $R(c)=(\sum_i c_ix_i,\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector by [L3], since its domain dimension is $N$ and its codomain dimension is $d+1$. Hence $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_ix_i=0$, with both signs among the $c_i$. If $\sum_i c_is(x_i)\ne0$, choose the sign of $c$ so that this sum is positive. For sufficiently small $t>0$, the weights $\theta_i+tc_i$ are nonnegative, preserve total mass and barycenter, and increase the last coordinate above $r_*$, contradicting maximality in step 3.2. Thus $\sum_i c_is(x_i)=0$. Now take $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. This removes at least one positive weight while preserving total mass, barycenter, and entropy value $r_*$. Repeating finitely many times leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights.

Let $P_*:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ be the probability measure from step 4.1. Each $\delta_{x_i}$ is countably additive because among disjoint Borel sets at most one contains $x_i$, and $\delta_{x_i}(K)=1$; hence $P_*$ is a Borel probability measure. It has barycenter $\bar x$ and entropy $r_*$, so it is feasible by the model assumption. For any other feasible Borel probability $P$, step 3.1 gives $(\bar x,\int s\,dP)\in C$, so $\int s\,dP\le r_*$. Thus $P_*$ attains the entropy maximum among all Borel mixtures and has at most $d+1$ atoms. No finite generator menu was assumed.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless generator coordinates. Each $x\in K$ labels one model-specified phase-generator state; the model assigns it entropy per mole $s(x)\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $s:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, using the numerical entropy value in that fixed unit. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ to be the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$. A Borel probability mixture is a countably additive probability measure $P$ on that sigma algebra; its barycenter and entropy per mole are the coordinatewise integrals $\int_Kx\,dP$ and $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless generator coordinates. Each $x\in K$ labels one model-specified phase-generator state; the model assigns it entropy per mole $s(x)\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $s:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, using the numerical entropy value in that fixed unit. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ to be the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$. A Borel probability mixture is a countably additive probability measure $P$ on that sigma algebra; its barycenter and entropy per mole are the coordinatewise integrals $\int_Kx\,dP$ and $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

   a compact subset of $Y$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Fix a system at a positive temperature $T_0$ and external pressure $p_0>0$. Internal reaction extents may vary in a declared feasible set, but no species crosses the system's outer boundary. The system contacts only an ideal thermal reservoir at $T_0$ and an ideal pressure store at $p_0$; all other work coordinates and excluded-energy changes are absent. Let $U$ be system internal energy in joules, $V$ volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $S$ system entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Define the constrained potential
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}:=U+p_0V-T_0S.
$$
For every admitted spontaneous endpoint change, $\Delta\Phi_{T_0,p_0}\le0$. If the system-plus-reservoir-plus-store endpoint is an attained global entropy maximum on its exact feasible set, then the corresponding system endpoint attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ over the induced feasible reaction states. This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

At fixed $t$, differentiating the rational equation gives
$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial v}=-\frac{24t}{(3v-1)^2}+\frac{6}{v^3}.
$$
At $t=0.9$ and $v=1$, this derivative is $-24(0.9)/4+6=0.6>0$.

The second derivative is $\partial_v^2p=144t/(3v-1)^3-18/v^4$. At a simultaneous zero, the first derivative gives $t=(3v-1)^2/(4v^3)$ and the second gives $t=(3v-1)^3/(8v^4)$. Equality and $v>1/3$ imply $2v=3v-1$, hence $v=1$, $t=1$, and $p=1$. Conversely these values make both derivatives zero. Thus $T_c$ is the model critical temperature in this stated sense, and $t=0.9<1$ is below it.

The derivative is continuous near $(t,v)=(0.9,1)$ because $3v-1\ne0$ there. Hence it remains positive on some open neighborhood within $v>1/3$. Since $P=P_cp$ and $V=V_cv$ with positive scales, $(\partial P/\partial V)_T=(P_c/V_c)(\partial p/\partial v)_t>0$ there as well. This verifies a positive-slope branch of this phenomenological model only.

Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.
